title: Two Roads to the Oscars: How Gondhal and Angh Both Entered the Race
excerpt: Gondhal is India's official Oscar submission, but Angh qualified independently through a new festival-award rule — putting two Indian films on separate tracks to the 2027 Academy Awards.
body:
• India has two horses in the 2027 Oscars race: Gondhal, the country's official submission, and Angh, which qualified independently through a new festival-award route.
  • Gondhal — a Marathi folk thriller by Santosh Davakhar — was chosen by the Film Federation of India from 33 contenders on September 19, becoming the first Marathi selection since Court in 2015.
  • Angh, Theja Rio's debut feature set in 1960s Nagaland, won the Platform Prize at the Toronto International Film Festival, which now grants independent entry to the International Feature race.
  • The Academy announces its 15-film shortlist on December 15, 2026, with nominations on January 21, 2027 — and India has precedent for multi-film success.

India is taking two roads to the 99th Academy Awards. On September 19, the Film Federation of India named Gondhal, a Marathi folk thriller, as the country's official entry for the 2027 Oscars. Days later, Angh — a debut feature from Nagaland — earned its own path to the same race by winning the Platform Prize at the Toronto International Film Festival. They are not rivals for one slot. Under new Academy rules, both films can legitimately chase Oscar gold.

Gondhal: the official entry

Gondhal was selected from 33 films vying for India's official submission, with Angh and the Sriram Raghavan-directed Ikkis reportedly among the top three contenders. Directed by Santosh Davakhar, the film is set in rural Maharashtra and unfolds around the Gondhal — a midnight ritual of folk performance and devotion. Ishita Deshmukh leads the cast, with music by the legendary Ilaiyaraaja.

"The selection is a landmark for Marathi cinema."

The selection is a landmark for Marathi cinema. Gondhal is only the fourth Marathi film ever chosen as India's official entry, after Shwaas (2004), Harishchandrachi Factory (2009) and Court (2015). It premiered at IFFI 2025, where Davakhar won the Silver Peacock for Best Director — early validation for a film that now carries the hopes of the world's largest film industry on the awards circuit.

Angh: the festival route

Angh arrives by a completely different road. Theja Rio's feature debut is set in 1960s Nagaland and follows a Konyak chief, the Anghba, and his family through a period of profound change. It was the only Indian film in competition in TIFF's Platform section this year, and it won the section's top prize from a jury led by Argentine filmmaker Pablo Trapero.

The film's cast pairs BAFTA winner Douglas Henshall with Indigenous Naga actors, and it is adapted from Rio's own 2021 short film. Its Toronto triumph did more than win a trophy — it unlocked the Oscars.

How both films can be in the race

This is where the Academy's rulebook matters. Ordinarily, each country submits a single film for the International Feature Film award — that is Gondhal's route, as India's official selection. But the Academy has introduced a parallel path: non-English-language films that win the top prize at six designated festivals — Berlin's Golden Bear, Busan's Best Film award, Cannes' Palme d'Or, Sundance's World Cinema Grand Jury Prize, Venice's Golden Lion, and Toronto's Platform Prize — can enter the International Feature race independently, provided they had a qualifying theatrical release between October 1, 2025 and September 30, 2026.

Angh's Platform Prize puts it squarely in that second lane. As Esquire India noted in its explainer, the two films are not competing for India's one slot — they are running on separate tracks toward the same shortlist. It is an unusual situation, but not an unprecedented one for Indian cinema at the Academy.

What happens next

The Academy will announce its 15-film International Feature shortlist on December 15, 2026, with the final five nominations following on January 21, 2027, ahead of the ceremony in March. India has recent precedent for a multi-film showing: at the 95th Academy Awards, the country fielded the official entry Chhello Show alongside All That Breathes, The Elephant Whisperers and the Naatu Naatu phenomenon — and walked away with two wins.

Whether Gondhal, Angh or both make the December shortlist, the symbolism is already significant. One film carries the establishment's endorsement through the official selection; the other earned its place purely on festival merit, from a region — Nagaland — that has rarely figured in India's awards-season conversation. Between them, they suggest an Indian cinema that is no longer betting on a single horse.

nri_angle: For the diaspora, it's a double stake in awards season — a Marathi folk thriller carrying India's official banner and a Naga story that reached the Oscars on its own festival merit.
